source.title: GASP: Efficient Black-Box Generation of Adversarial Suffixes for Jailbreaking LLMs

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates whether adversarial suffixes appended to harmful requests elicit harmful responses from safety-trained chat models. It tests suffix attacks directly, but does not test the first-token mechanism or fine-tuning claims.
record.gate_note: The reported attack-success rates for GASP suffixes bear on V4. Results comparing the study's attack method with other attacks, the LBO and evaluator ablations, and readability or efficiency metrics are not included as rows because they do not independently measure the claim versions. Table 3's flattened values could not be assigned reliably to model, dataset, and method, so they are not extracted.
record.test_reason: This is a jailbreak-method paper. GASP trains a suffix generator and reports its own attack-success rates against baselines (Table 2, Table 3, Fig. 3). It reports no no-attack refusal baseline and does not examine response openings, prefilling or decoding. Its rows measure how well the authors' method performs, not whether getting past the opening defeats safety, so it relies on suffix jailbreaking as a tool rather than testing V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that GASP efficiently generates human-readable adversarial suffixes in a fully black-box setting, with higher ASR than baselines across open, closed (e.g. GPT-4o 47%, Claude-3.7-Sonnet 59% ASR@10) and defended models. They also report lower training and inference cost. They stress that ASR depends strongly on the evaluator.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains a suffix generator on an adversarial-suffix dataset, then uses latent Bayesian optimization and ORPO feedback to adapt generated suffixes to target models. It does not use the original fine-tuning or first-token KL measurement recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR varies across target models, evaluators, defense settings, and ASR@1 versus ASR@10.

fits_no_version.finding: App. F.5 reports that GASP suffixes elicit harmful content wrapped in built-in warnings on LLaMA-2/3. It contrasts this with GCG/DAN, which force a fixed compliant opening such as "Sure, here is". This is a qualitative observation with no rates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Readable suffix jailbreaks can elicit harmful content without a compliant opening, alongside safety disclaimers.

record.problems: The paper reports medians over three runs but no error bars or significance tests. The reported ASR varies considerably by evaluator and target model; the authors also describe some evaluator-specific misclassification issues.
record.rows_left_out: Table 3 results are not extracted because the provided flattened text does not support reliable assignment of its values to each model, dataset, and method. Figure 3b's other defense-setting values are not transcribed because their individual labels and values are not reliably recoverable from the flattened figure text; the explicit defense results stated in Section 4.2 are included.

untested.parts: Not studied: harmful fine-tuning of target models.
Not studied: benign fine-tuning of target models.
Not studied: per-token KL across response positions.
Prefilling, decoding changes, and whether suffixes work by getting past the opening tokens; no unattacked baseline is reported.
Not studied: localization of safety in parameters.

record.verdict_notes: Classified as T4 because every row is the authors' own attack's performance, and no refusal baseline without the attack is given. The record's V4 labels relied on these method-performance rows, so they are dropped. Table 2 values were checked and match. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning data and its effect on refusal.
Benign fine-tuning data and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across response positions.

The study tests its generated adversarial suffixes, but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes. It does not isolate a general causal effect of merely getting past the first response tokens.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens and whether such training remains effective.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: GASP suffix attacks, especially ASR@10 under StrongREJECT or GASPEval and the reported defended-model cases
reader_labels.reason: Suffix attacks produce harmful-completion ASRs in these conditions; see r3-r6, r9-r12, r17-r18, r23-r24, r27-r30, and r33-r34.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Results vary by model, evaluator, and attempt count
reader_labels.reason: Some ASRs are low or zero, particularly on LLaMA models under Keyword Matching, while rates differ substantially across evaluators and between ASR@1 and ASR@10; see r13-r16, r19-r22, and r25-r28.
